title: HiMAE: Hierarchical Masked Autoencoders Discover Resolution-Specific Structure in Wearable Time Series
claim: A single masked-autoencoding U-Net yields multi-resolution embeddings that feed linear probes, so one pipeline probes which temporal scales support each downstream task.
layout: Numbered 5-stage flow, left-to-right across the top (input, masking, U-Net, reconstruction), then a bottom row for evaluation and a task list. Dotted lines drop from encoder layers to the evaluation block.
description: A numbered five-step diagram. The top row runs left to right. Step 1 is four waveform patches. Step 2 shows the same patches with some blacked out. Next is a large U-Net drawn as 3D trapezoid blocks, with blue encoders (Encoder 1–3) on the left and green decoders (Decoder 1–3) on the right. Skip-connection lines arch over the blocks. Step 3 shows the reconstructed patches, with dashed blue curves filling the masked ones, labeled 'Generative Task'. Dotted lines drop from the encoder bottlenecks to step 4, Evaluation. That row runs left to right: waveforms at three receptive-field scales (L1–L3), embedding bars, linear probes, and metric bar charts, linked by black arrows. Step 5 on the right lists Sleep Staging, Abnormal Labs and Cardiovascular Conditions as cards with icons, grouped by brackets into Classification and Regression tasks. Blue and green gradients carry the eye first, then the black arrows.
caption: HiMAE pre-training and evaluation pipeline. (1) Physiological sequences are split into temporal patches. (2) Selected patches are masked randomly or contiguously. (3) A U-Net–style CNN encoder–decoder reconstructs missing values, with loss applied only to masked regions. (4) Multi-resolution embeddings feed linear probes for classification and regression benchmarking. (5) Three categorized task-lists are evaluated.
abstract: Wearable sensors provide abundant physiological time series, yet the principles governing their predictive utility remain unclear. We hypothesize that temporal resolution is a fundamental axis of representation learning, with different clinical and behavioral outcomes relying on structure at distinct scales. To test this resolution hypothesis, we introduce HiMAE (Hierarchical Masked Autoencoder), a self supervised framework that combines masked autoencoding with a hierarchical convolutional encoder decoder. HiMAE produces multi resolution embeddings that enable systematic evaluation of which temporal scales carry predictive signal, transforming resolution from a hyperparameter into a probe for interpretability. Across classification, regression, and generative benchmarks, HiMAE consistently outperforms state of the art foundation models that collapse scale, while being orders of magnitude smaller. HiMAE is an efficient representation learner compact enough to run entirely on watch, achieving sub millisecond inference on smartwatch class CPUs for true edge inference. Together, these contributions position HiMAE as both an efficient self supervised learning method and a discovery tool for scale sensitive structure in wearable health.
